Speaker: Merel van Goch @merelvg

Affiliation: Radboud University

Title: Once upon a time in academia: how shared reading of campus novels fosters PhD candidates’ wellbeing

Abstract: The well-being of PhD candidates is under pressure; many of them experience imposter feelings. Reading for pleasure increases people’s well-being: Stories, and especially humor in stories, can help people by creating reflective distance from reality. We hypothesize that campus novels – novels set on college campuses, told from the perspectives of faculty or students – are particularly effective, because they are characterized by dark humor and satire. We let groups of PhD candidates reflect on campus novel texts together, and study the interaction between texts and readers, and the effects of group reflection on well-being.

Long abstract

Problem: compromised well-being of PhD candidates
Well-being and work enjoyment of PhD candidates are under pressure. Many PhD candidates experience imposter feelings [1]: fear of exposure of one’s intellectual or creative shortcomings, belief in one’s unsuitability for an academic position, the inability to internalize accomplishments, and the belief that others in one’s research and personal communities are blind to these apparent and disqualifying shortcomings [2]. The difficult professional, academic and emotional contexts of an early academic career are related to the quality-of-life challenges confronting PhD candidates. Indeed, obtaining a doctorate is challenging. PhD candidates are expected to work independently and under high pressure, and the limited career prospects within academia create intense competition and uncertainty. Often this creates a work-environment brimming with unclear expectations, boundaries, tasks, roles, and prospects for job security [1]. Imposter feelings are negatively correlated with overall mental health, and positively correlated with anxiety and psychological distress. This not only negatively affects PhD candidates’ well-being and work, but also higher education and society at large, because decreased well-being negatively influences cognitive, emotional and social aspects. It is therefore important for individuals, academia and society to find solutions to this problem. This project explores a solution in the form of reflection through literature, and specifically literature about academia. Research has shown that reading for pleasure increases people’s well-being by helping them cope better with stress [3].
Potential solution: reflecting on campus novels
Literature helps us reflect on ourselves and our lives. People engage with narratives to get a temporary relief from the task of maintenance, defense, and regulation of the personal and social self [4]. By reading fiction, the boundaries of self are expanded, and the reader is not limited to rules of social norms or morality. Immersion in stories helps to disconnect from daily life: they help us see our possible selves, and possible roles we can have at work [5]. In the current project, we hypothesize that campus novels are particularly effective for such reflection, because these novels are often characterized by dark humor and satire [6; 7], and humor can help keep or create reflective distance from reality [8]. Campus novels are set in and around college campuses and told from the perspectives of faculty members or students. Popular examples are Nabokov’s Pnin, Tartt’s The Secret History and Williams’ Stoner.
To elicit reflection, we use the method shared reading: a specific literary activity in which a group reads and reflects on a text, with a “reader leader” guiding the conversation [9; 10]. This evidence-based low-cost and low-threshold way to improve mental well-being of different target groups finds its success in communal meaning-making processes and collaboration. Dimensions of participants’ experiences that contribute to the positive effects are: 1) an open space; 2) disconnecting through connecting:, 3) community, and 4) resonances and echoes [10]. Reflecting on campus novels through the method of shared reading can be seen as a form of reflection-on-action [11], a small intervention in scholars’ practice. Regular systematic reflection on their work, and what it means to them, can bring ample benefits to scholars’ academic and personal lives.
The project’s research question is: How can reading and reflecting on campus novels relieve imposter feelings of PhD candidates?
Study I aims to identify insights into the dynamics of reader responses for future successful implementations of the shared reading program targeting PhD candidates with the objective to positively affect their well-being in general and at work. A group of 5-8 PhD candidates reads and reflects on texts together, using the shared reading paradigm, guided by a reader leader, who invites participants to reflect at specific moments [9; 10; 12]. We use the qualitative analysis method grounded theory to theorise about how fiction can relieve imposter feelings: what triggers an optimal psychological distance? What role might fictionality and humor play in this respect?
Study II explores the effects of the shared reading sessions as an intervention, using a pretest-posttest design and quantitative methods. We measure participants’ perceived stress [13], imposter feelings [2], anxiety [14], and well-being at work [15] before and after the intervention. The intervention entails reading and reflecting on texts in groups of 5-8 PhD candidates, guided by a reader leader. Specific hypotheses and/or measures of Study 2 depend on the outcomes of Study 1. A potential focus could be: how can the psychological distance to the reader’s self be optimised through humor? What is the relationship between different types of humor and the extent to which the reading experience determines a psychological distance from the events?
